title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: "Finally, it's over, thank God!" was Anna Arkadyevna's first thought once she'd said her last goodbye to her brother, who'd stood blocking the carriage entrance until the third bell rang. She sat down on her seat beside Annushka and looked around at the dim twilight of the sleeping car. "Thank God! Tomorrow I'll see Seryozha and Alexey Alexandrovitch, and my life will go back to normal, all nice and the same as always."

She'd been anxious all day, and that same restlessness stayed with her as she settled in for the journey, taking great care over every detail. Her small, deft hands opened and closed her little red bag, pulled out a cushion, set it on her lap, and wrapped her feet snugly before she made herself comfortable. An invalid lady nearby had already lain down to sleep. Two other women struck up a conversation with Anna, and a heavyset older lady tucked her feet under her and complained about how the train was heated. Anna answered with a few words, but seeing no real entertainment in the conversation, she asked Annushka to fetch her a lamp, hung it on the arm of her seat, and took a paper-knife and an English novel from her bag. At first she couldn't get into her reading. The commotion around her was distracting; then, once the train got moving, she found herself listening to its noises; then it was the snow beating against the left-hand window and sticking to the glass, the sight of the bundled-up guard walking past, covered in snow on one side, and the talk around her about the terrible blizzard outside — all of it pulled her attention away. Farther on, it was the same thing over and over: the same jolting and rattling, the same snow on the window, the same quick swings from stifling heat to cold and back to heat again, the same passing glimpses of the same shapes in the half-light, the same voices — and Anna finally began to read and actually take in what she was reading. Annushka was already dozing, the red bag in her lap held by her broad, gloved hands, one glove torn. Anna Arkadyevna read and understood what she read, but she found it distasteful — following the reflected lives of other people. She wanted too badly to live her own life. If she read that the novel's heroine was nursing a sick man, she wanted to be the one moving quietly around a sickroom herself; if she read about a member of Parliament giving a speech, she wanted to be the one giving it; if she read about how Lady Mary had ridden to hounds, provoked her sister-in-law, and shocked everyone with her nerve, she too wished she were doing the same. But there was nothing to actually do, so she kept twisting the smooth paper-knife in her hands and forced herself to read.

The novel's hero was already nearly at his English version of happiness — a baronetcy and an estate — and Anna felt a wish to go there with him, when she suddenly sensed that _he_ ought to feel ashamed, and that she was ashamed of the very same thing. But what did he have to be ashamed of? "What do I have to be ashamed of?" she asked herself, stung and surprised. She set the book down and sank back against the chair, gripping the paper-cutter tightly in both hands. There was nothing. She went back through all her memories of Moscow. They were all good, pleasant ones. She remembered the ball, remembered Vronsky's face full of slavish adoration, remembered everything about how she'd behaved with him — none of it was shameful. And yet, at that very point in her memories, the feeling of shame grew sharper, as though some inner voice, right when she thought of Vronsky, were telling her, "Warm, very warm, hot." "Well, what is it, then?" she said to herself firmly, shifting her position on the seat. "What does it mean? Am I afraid to look it straight in the face? What is it, really? Is it possible that something exists — or could ever exist — between me and this boy of an officer, beyond the ordinary relations one has with any acquaintance?" She laughed contemptuously and picked her book back up, but now she genuinely couldn't follow what she was reading. She ran the paper-knife along the windowpane, then pressed its smooth, cool surface to her cheek, and almost laughed out loud at the wave of delight that suddenly came over her for no reason at all. She felt as if her nerves were strings being wound tighter and tighter on some kind of screw peg. Her eyes felt like they were opening wider and wider, her fingers and toes twitched nervously, something inside her chest pressed down on her breathing, and in the uncertain half-light every shape and sound struck her with unusual vividness. Moments of doubt kept coming over her — she'd lose track of whether the train was moving forward, moving backward, or standing still altogether; whether it was Annushka beside her or a stranger. "What's that on the arm of the chair — a fur cloak, or some animal? And what am I myself? Am I myself, or some other woman?" She was afraid of giving in to this half-delirious state. But something pulled her toward it, and she could choose to yield to it or resist it. She got up to shake herself out of it, and slipped off her plaid wrap and the cape of her warm dress. For a moment she came back to herself and realized that the thin peasant who'd just come in, wearing a long overcoat with buttons missing, was the stove-tender, that he was checking the thermometer, that it was the wind and snow blowing in behind him through the door — but then everything blurred again... That long-waisted peasant seemed to be gnawing at something on the wall; the old lady began stretching her legs the whole length of the carriage, filling it with a black cloud; then came a terrible shrieking and banging, as if someone were being torn apart; then a blinding flash of red fire before her eyes, and a wall seemed to rise up and hide everything. Anna felt as though she were sinking down. But it wasn't frightening — it was delightful. A man's voice, muffled and covered in snow, shouted something close to her ear. She sat up and pulled herself together; she realized they'd reached a station, and that this was the guard. She asked Annushka to hand her the cape she'd taken off, along with her shawl, put them on, and moved toward the door.
"Do you want to get off?" asked Annushka.
"Yes, I want some air. It's so hot in here." And she opened the door. The driving snow and wind rushed at her, fighting her for control of the door. But she found she was enjoying the struggle.

She pushed the door open and went out. The wind seemed to have been lying in wait for her; with a gleeful whistle it tried to snatch her up and carry her off, but she clung to the cold doorpost and, holding her skirt, made her way down onto the platform and into the shelter of the cars. The wind had been fierce on the steps, but here on the platform, sheltered by the carriages, it had died down. With real pleasure she breathed in deep lungfuls of the freezing, snow-scented air, and, standing near the carriage, took in the platform and the lit-up station around her.

title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch got back from the ministers' meeting at four o'clock, but as usual, he didn't have time to stop in and see her. He went straight to his study to see the people waiting on him with petitions, and to sign papers his chief secretary had brought him. By dinnertime (the Karenins always had a few people over) an old lady had arrived — a cousin of Alexey Alexandrovitch's — along with the chief secretary of the department and his wife, and a young man who'd been recommended to Alexey Alexandrovitch for a position. Anna went into the drawing room to greet the guests. At exactly five o'clock, before the bronze Peter the Great clock had finished striking the fifth chime, Alexey Alexandrovitch came in wearing a white tie and evening coat with two decorations, since he had to leave right after dinner. Every minute of Alexey Alexandrovitch's life was scheduled and accounted for. To make time for everything he had to get through each day, he stuck to the strictest punctuality. "Without haste, without rest" was his motto. He came into the dining room, greeted everyone, and sat down quickly, smiling at his wife.
"Yes, my solitude is over. You wouldn't believe how uncomfortable" (he put emphasis on the word _uncomfortable_) "it is to eat dinner alone."

Over dinner he talked a little with his wife about Moscow matters and, with a sarcastic smile, asked after Stepan Arkadyevitch; but for the most part the conversation stayed general, covering Petersburg official and public news. After dinner he spent half an hour with the guests, then again pressed his wife's hand with a smile, excused himself, and drove off to the council meeting. Anna didn't go out that evening — not to Princess Betsy Tverskaya's, who'd invited her as soon as she heard she was back, and not to the theater, where she had a box reserved for that night. Mainly she stayed in because the dress she'd been counting on wasn't ready. Once her guests had left and she turned her attention to her wardrobe, she was thoroughly annoyed. She was usually skilled at dressing well without spending much, and before leaving Moscow she'd given her dressmaker three dresses to alter. They were supposed to be transformed beyond recognition and ready three days earlier. It turned out two of them hadn't been touched at all, and the third hadn't been altered the way Anna wanted. The dressmaker came to explain herself, insisting her version was better, and Anna got so furious that she felt ashamed about it afterward, looking back. To calm herself down completely, she went to the nursery and spent the whole evening with her son, put him to bed herself, made the sign of the cross over him, and tucked him in. She was glad she hadn't gone out anywhere, and had spent the evening this way instead. She felt light-hearted and at peace, and could see clearly that everything that had seemed so important on her train journey was only one of the ordinary, trivial incidents of fashionable life, and that she had no reason to feel ashamed in front of anyone else, or in front of herself. Anna sat down by the fire with an English novel and waited for her husband. At exactly half past nine she heard his ring, and he came into the room.
"There you are, finally!" she said, holding out her hand to him.
He kissed her hand and sat down beside her.
"So, overall, I take it your trip was a success," he said to her.

"Oh, yes," she said, and started telling him everything from the beginning — her trip with Countess Vronskaya, her arrival, the accident at the station. Then she described the pity she'd felt, first for her brother, and afterward for Dolly.
"I don't think one can let a man like that off the hook, even if he is your brother," Alexey Alexandrovitch said sternly.
Anna smiled. She knew he said that only to show that family loyalty couldn't stop him from stating his honest opinion. She recognized that trait in her husband, and she liked it.
"I'm glad it's all worked out so well, and that you're back again," he went on. "So, what are they saying about the new act I got passed in the council?"
Anna hadn't heard anything about this act, and she felt a pang of guilt that she'd so easily forgotten something that mattered so much to him.
"Well, here it's caused quite a stir," he said, with a self-satisfied smile.

She could tell Alexey Alexandrovitch wanted to tell her something that pleased him about it, so she drew it out of him with questions. With the same self-satisfied smile, he told her about the praise he'd received for the act he'd pushed through.
"I was very, very pleased. It shows that a sensible, steady view of the matter is finally taking hold among us."
After finishing his second cup of tea with cream, and some bread, Alexey Alexandrovitch got up and started toward his study.
"And you didn't go out anywhere tonight? I imagine you were bored?" he said.
"Oh, not at all!" she answered, standing up to follow him across the room to his study. "What are you reading these days?" she asked.
"Right now I'm reading Duc de Lille's _Poésie des Enfers_," he answered. "A remarkable book."

Anna smiled — the way people smile at the small flaws of someone they love — and, slipping her hand under his arm, walked him to the study door. She knew his habit of reading in the evening, a habit that had become a necessity for him. She also knew that, despite his official duties, which ate up nearly all his time, he considered it his duty to stay current on everything significant happening in the intellectual world. She knew, too, that he genuinely cared about books on politics, philosophy, and theology, and that art meant nothing to him by nature; yet despite that — or maybe because of it — Alexey Alexandrovitch never let anything in the art world go unread, and made a point of getting through all of it. She knew that in politics, philosophy, and theology he often had doubts and looked into things further; but on questions of art and poetry, and especially music, which he had no understanding of whatsoever, he held the most firm and settled opinions. He loved talking about Shakespeare, Raphael, and Beethoven, and about the significance of new schools of poetry and music — all of which he sorted and classified with remarkably conspicuous consistency.
"Well, God be with you," she said at the door of the study, where a shaded candle and a carafe of water had already been set beside his armchair. "And I'll write to Moscow."
He pressed her hand, and kissed it again.

"Still, he's a good man — honest, kind-hearted, and quite accomplished in his own field," Anna told herself as she went back to her room, as though she were defending him to someone who'd attacked him and claimed he couldn't be loved. "But why do his ears stick out so oddly? Or did he just get a haircut?"

At exactly twelve o'clock, while Anna was still at her writing table finishing a letter to Dolly, she heard the steady shuffle of slippers, and Alexey Alexandrovitch came in, freshly washed and combed, a book under his arm.
"Time for bed, time for bed," he said, with a knowing smile, and went into their bedroom.
"And what right did he have to look at him like that?" Anna thought, remembering the way Vronsky had glanced at Alexey Alexandrovitch.

As she undressed and went into the bedroom, her face showed none of the eagerness that, during her stay in Moscow, had fairly flashed from her eyes and her smile; if anything, the fire in her seemed quenched now, tucked away somewhere far out of reach.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: From then on, a new kind of life began for Alexey Alexandrovitch and his wife. Nothing dramatic happened. Anna kept going out in society as she always had, was especially often at Princess Betsy's, and ran into Vronsky everywhere. Alexey Alexandrovitch saw it, but there was nothing he could do about it. Every attempt he made to draw her into an open conversation ran up against a wall he couldn't get through — a kind of amused bewilderment on her part. On the surface, nothing had changed, but underneath, their relationship was completely different. Alexey Alexandrovitch, a man with real power in the world of politics, found himself powerless here. Like an ox with its head lowered, he waited submissively for the blow he sensed hanging over him. Every time he thought about it, he told himself he had to try once more — that kindness, tenderness, and persuasion might still save her, might still bring her back to herself — and every day he got ready to talk to her. But every time he actually started, he felt that the same spirit of deceit and wrongdoing that had taken hold of her had taken hold of him too, and he ended up speaking to her in a completely different tone than he'd meant to use. Without meaning to, he fell into his habitual tone of mocking anyone who said what he was about to say. And in that tone, there was no way to say what actually needed to be said to her.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: What had been, for almost a full year, Vronsky's one consuming desire — replacing every desire he'd had before — and what had been for Anna an impossible, terrifying, and precisely for that reason even more intoxicating dream of happiness — that desire was now fulfilled. He stood before her, pale, his lower jaw trembling, begging her to calm down, without knowing how or why.
"Anna! Anna!" he said, his voice breaking, "Anna, for God's sake!..."

But the louder he spoke, the lower she bent her head — once proud and lighthearted, now overcome with shame — and she slid down from the sofa where she'd been sitting, sinking to the floor at his feet; she would have collapsed onto the carpet if he hadn't caught her.
"My God! Forgive me!" she said, sobbing, pressing his hands against her chest.

She felt so sinful, so guilty, that there was nothing left for her to do but humble herself and beg forgiveness; and since there was no one else left in her life but him, it was to him that she directed her plea. Looking at him, she felt her humiliation almost as a physical thing, and she couldn't say anything more. He felt what a murderer must feel looking at the body he's just taken the life from. That body — the life he'd taken from it — was their love, the first stage of it. There was something horrifying and repulsive in remembering what had been bought at this terrible price of shame. Shame at their bared, naked souls crushed her and spread to him. But despite all the murderer's horror at the sight of his victim's body, he had to cut it up, hide it, make use of what his crime had won him.

And with something like fury, almost like passion — the way a murderer falls on the body and drags and hacks at it — that's how he covered her face and shoulders with kisses. She held his hand and didn't move. "Yes — these kisses, this is what's been bought with this shame. Yes, and this one hand, which will always be mine — the hand of my accomplice." She lifted that hand and kissed it. He dropped to his knees, trying to see her face, but she hid it and said nothing. Finally, as if forcing herself, she stood up and pushed him away. Her face was still beautiful, but only more pitiful for it.
"It's over," she said. "I have nothing left but you. Remember that."
"I could never forget what is now my whole life. For one moment of this happiness..."
"Happiness!" she said, with horror and disgust, and her horror passed into him without her meaning it to. "For pity's sake — not a word, not another word."
She got up quickly and moved away from him.

"Not another word," she repeated, and with a look of cold despair he couldn't understand, she left him. She felt that at that moment she couldn't put into words the shame, the rapture, and the horror of stepping into this new life, and she didn't want to talk about it — didn't want to cheapen the feeling with the wrong words. But later, too — the next day, and the day after that — she still couldn't find the words to capture the tangle of what she felt; she couldn't even find the thoughts to think it through clearly in her own mind.

She told herself: "No, I can't think about it right now — later, when I'm calmer." But that calm never came; every time the thought rose up of what she'd done, of what would happen to her, of what she ought to do, a wave of horror swept over her and she pushed the thoughts away.
"Later, later," she said — "when I'm calmer."

But in her dreams, where she had no control over her own thoughts, her situation showed itself to her in its full, ugly nakedness. One dream came to her almost every night. She dreamed that both men were her husbands at once, that both were showering her with affection. Alexey Alexandrovitch was crying, kissing her hands, saying, "How happy we are now!" And Alexey Vronsky was there too, and he was her husband as well. And she marveled that it had ever seemed impossible, explaining to them, laughing, that it was really so much simpler than that, and that now they were all happy and content. But the dream weighed on her like a nightmare, and she'd wake from it in terror.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: In the first days after coming back from Moscow, whenever Levin flinched and flushed, remembering the humiliation of being turned down, he told himself: "This is exactly how I used to flinch and blush, thinking I was completely done for, when I flunked physics and didn't get promoted; and how I thought myself completely ruined after I'd botched that business of my sister's that had been entrusted to me. And yet now, years later, I look back on it and I'm amazed it could have upset me so much. It'll be the same with this trouble. Time will pass, and I won't care about this either."

But three months had gone by and he still hadn't stopped caring about it; it was just as painful to think about as it had been in those first days. He couldn't find any peace, because after dreaming for so long about family life, feeling himself so ready for it, he still wasn't married, and was further from marriage than ever. He was painfully aware, as everyone around him was too, that at his age it isn't good for a man to be alone. He remembered how, before he'd left for Moscow, he'd once told his cowman Nikolay — a simple, good-hearted peasant he liked talking to — "Well, Nikolay, I mean to get married," and how Nikolay had shot back immediately, as if it were a matter beyond any doubt: "And high time too, Konstantin Dmitrievitch." But marriage was now further away than ever. The place was taken, and whenever he tried to picture any of the women he knew stepping into it, he felt it was simply impossible. On top of that, the memory of the rejection, and the part he'd played in it, tormented him with shame. However often he told himself he wasn't really to blame for it, that memory — like other humiliating memories of the same kind — made him wince and flush. There had been things in his past, as in anyone's, that he recognized as genuinely bad, things his conscience ought to have tormented him over; but the memory of those bad actions never caused him anything like the suffering that these small, humiliating memories did. Those wounds never healed. And now his rejection, and the pitiful figure he must have cut in front of everyone that evening, had joined the ranks of those memories. But time and work did their part. The bitter memories were increasingly buried under the incidents of country life — petty in his eyes, but genuinely important. Every week he thought about Kitty a little less. He waited impatiently for news that she was married, or just about to be, hoping that such news would, like pulling a bad tooth, cure him completely.

Meanwhile spring arrived, beautiful and kind, without spring's usual delays and false starts — one of those rare springs where plants, animals, and people all rejoice together. This lovely spring stirred Levin up even more, and strengthened his resolve to give up his whole past and build a solitary life for himself, solid and independent. Though many of the plans he'd brought back to the country with him hadn't come to anything, his most important resolution — staying pure — had held. He was free of the shame that usually weighed on him after a lapse, and he could look anyone straight in the eye. In February he'd gotten a letter from Marya Nikolaevna telling him his brother Nikolay's health was getting worse, but that he wouldn't listen to advice; on the strength of that letter, Levin had gone to Moscow to see his brother and managed to convince him to see a doctor and go abroad to take the waters. He'd done such a good job persuading his brother, and lending him money for the trip without making him bristle, that he felt genuinely pleased with himself over it. On top of his farm work, which needed special attention that spring, and on top of his reading, Levin had started, that winter, a book on agriculture — one built around treating the character of the farm laborer as an unchangeable given of the problem, on the same footing as climate and soil, and deriving all the principles of scientific farming not just from data on soil and climate, but from data on soil, climate, and a certain fixed character of the laborer. So even in his solitude — or maybe because of it — his life felt remarkably full. Only rarely did he feel the itch to share his stray ideas with someone besides Agafea Mihalovna. And with her, in fact, he'd fall into arguments fairly often about physics, farming theory, and especially philosophy — philosophy being Agafea Mihalovna's favorite subject.

Spring took its time arriving. For the last few weeks the weather had stayed steadily clear and frosty. It thawed in the sun during the day, but at night the temperature dropped as low as seven degrees below freezing. The crust on the snow was hard enough that wagons could be driven anywhere, off the roads entirely. Easter came with the snow still down. Then, all at once, on Easter Monday, a warm wind picked up, storm clouds rolled in, and for three days and three nights warm rain poured down in sheets. On Thursday the wind died and a thick gray fog settled over the land, as if hiding whatever transformations were taking place underneath. Behind the fog came the sound of running water, the cracking and drifting of ice, the rush of muddy, foaming torrents; and the following Monday evening, the fog broke apart, the storm clouds split into little curling wisps, the sky cleared, and real spring had arrived. In the morning the sun rose bright and quickly burned off the thin layer of ice covering the water, and the warm air shimmered with steam rising from the reviving earth. The old grass looked greener, and new blades pushed up through it; the buds on the guelder-rose, the currant bushes, and the sticky birch buds swelled with sap, and a scouting bee hummed around the golden blossoms dotting the willow. Larks trilled somewhere unseen above the velvety green fields and the ice-crusted stubble; lapwings cried over the low, flooded marshland; cranes and wild geese flew high overhead, calling out their spring cries. Cattle, patchy where their new coats hadn't grown in yet, lowed in the pastures; bow-legged lambs frisked around their bleating mothers. Barefoot children ran along the drying paths, leaving their footprints behind. Peasant women chattered cheerfully by the pond as they washed linen, and axes rang out in the yard where the men repaired ploughs and harrows. Real spring had come.

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Levin pulled on his big boots, and — for the first time — a cloth jacket instead of his fur coat, and went out to check on his farm, stepping over streams of water that flashed in the sunlight and dazzled his eyes, treading on ice one moment and sinking into sticky mud the next.

Spring is the season for plans and projects. And as he stepped out into the farmyard, Levin — like a tree in spring that has no idea what shape its young shoots and twigs, still locked inside swelling buds, will eventually take — barely knew what projects he was about to launch into on the farm work he loved so much. But he felt full of the most brilliant plans and schemes. First he went to check on the cattle. The cows had been let out into their paddock, their smooth flanks already gleaming with their new, sleek spring coats; they basked in the sun and lowed to be let out to the meadow. Levin looked over the cows he knew so intimately, down to the smallest detail of their condition, admiring them, and gave the order to drive them out to the meadow and let the calves into the paddock. The herdsman ran off happily to get the meadow ready. The dairymaids, hiking up their skirts, went splashing through the mud on bare legs — still winter-pale, not yet tanned by the sun — waving branches as they chased the calves, who frolicked in the giddiness of spring.

After admiring that year's young stock, which were unusually fine — the early calves were already the size of a peasant's cow, and Pava's daughter, at three months old, was as big as a yearling — Levin gave orders for a trough to be brought out so they could be fed in the paddock. But it turned out that since the paddock hadn't been used all winter, the fencing put up for it the autumn before had broken down. He sent for the carpenter, who by rights should have been working on the threshing machine. But it turned out the carpenter was busy fixing the harrows, which should have been repaired before Lent. This was extremely annoying to Levin. It was maddening to run into that same old sloppiness in the farm work that he'd been fighting against with everything he had for years now. The fencing, he learned, hadn't been needed over the winter, so it had been carried off to the cart-horse stable, and there it had broken, being lightly built and meant only for feeding calves. What's more, it turned out that the harrows and all the farm equipment he'd ordered checked over and repaired during the winter — for which he'd specifically hired three carpenters — hadn't been fixed at all, and the harrows were only now being repaired when they should already have been out working the fields. Levin sent for his bailiff, but immediately went out looking for him himself. The bailiff, beaming like everyone else that day, wearing a sheepskin coat trimmed with astrakhan, came out of the barn twisting a bit of straw between his fingers.
"Why isn't the carpenter working on the threshing machine?"
"Oh, I meant to tell you yesterday — the harrows need fixing. It's about time they got out into the fields."
"So what were they doing all winter, then?"
"But what did you need the carpenter for?"
"Where's the fencing for the calves' paddock?"
"I told them to get it ready. What can you do with peasants like these?" the bailiff said, waving his hand.

"It's not the peasants — it's this bailiff!" Levin snapped, losing his temper. "What exactly am I paying you for?" he shouted. But realizing that wouldn't fix anything, he cut himself off mid-sentence and just sighed. "Well — can we start sowing?" he asked after a pause.
"Behind Turkin, tomorrow or the day after, they could start."
"And the clover?"
"I've sent Vassily and Mishka — they're sowing now. I just don't know if they'll manage it, it's so muddy."
"How many acres?"
"About fifteen."
"Why not sow all of it?" Levin demanded.

That they were only sowing fifteen acres of clover, not all forty-five, bothered him even more. Clover, as he knew both from books and from his own experience, never did well unless it was sown as early as possible — practically while there was still snow on the ground. And yet Levin could never manage to get it done in time.
"There's no one to send. What can you do with a set of peasants like this? Three of them didn't even show up. And then there's Semyon..."
"Well, you should have pulled some men off the thatching."
"I did, actually."
"Then where are the peasants?"
"Five are making compôte" (meaning compost), "four are moving the oats because they're worried about mildew, Konstantin Dmitrievitch."
Levin knew perfectly well that "worried about mildew" meant his English seed oats were already ruined. Once again, they hadn't done what he'd told them.
"But I told you back during Lent to lay the drainage pipes!" he shouted.
"Don't worry — we'll get it all done in time."

Levin waved his hand angrily, went into the granary to check on the oats, then on to the stable. The oats weren't spoiled yet. But the peasants were carrying them out by the shovelful when they could have just let them slide down into the lower granary; after arranging for that to be done, and pulling two workers off that job to sow clover instead, Levin's irritation with the bailiff faded. It really was such a beautiful day that it was hard to stay angry.
"Ignat!" he called to the coachman, who was washing the carriage wheels with his sleeves rolled up. "Saddle up..."
"Which one, sir?"
"Kolpik, let's say."
"Yes, sir."

While the horse was being saddled, Levin called the bailiff back over — he was still hanging around nearby — to smooth things over, and started talking to him about the spring work ahead and his plans for the farm.

The wagons were to start hauling manure earlier, so it would all be finished before the early mowing began. The ploughing of the far land was to continue without interruption, so it could sit and ripen fallow. And the mowing was all to be done with hired labor, not on a profit-sharing basis. The bailiff listened closely and clearly made an effort to seem supportive of his employer's plans. But he still had that look Levin knew so well and that always irritated him — a look of hopelessness and gloom. That look said: "That's all well and good, but it's up to God."

Nothing frustrated Levin more than that tone. But it was the tone every bailiff he'd ever had used. They'd all taken that same attitude toward his plans, and so by now it didn't so much anger him as sting him, and it pushed him even harder to fight against what felt like some elemental force always working against him, one he could describe no other way than "as God wills."
"If we can manage it, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the bailiff said.
"Why wouldn't you manage it?"
"We really need another fifteen laborers. And they're just not showing up. There were some here today asking seventy roubles for the summer."

Levin fell silent. Once again he was up against that same opposing force. He knew that no matter how hard they tried, they couldn't hire more than forty laborers — maybe thirty-seven or thirty-eight — for a reasonable wage. About forty had already been taken on, and there weren't any more to be had. But still, he couldn't help pushing against it.
"Send someone to Sury, to Tchefirovka — if they won't come, we'll have to look elsewhere."
"Oh, I'll send someone, don't worry," Vassily Fedorovitch said gloomily. "But the horses aren't much good either."

"We'll get more. I know, of course," Levin added, laughing, "you always want to get by with as little as possible, and the worst quality you can manage — but this year I'm not letting you have your way. I'll see to everything myself."
"Well, I don't think you rest much as it is. It cheers us up, working under the master's eye..."
"So they're sowing clover behind Birch Dale? I'll go take a look," he said, mounting the little bay cob, Kolpik, who'd been brought over by the coachman.
"You won't be able to cross the streams, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the coachman called out.
"Fine, I'll go around by the forest."

And Levin rode through the mud of the farmyard, out through the gate and into the open country, his good little horse — after being cooped up so long — stepping out boldly, snorting over the puddles, seeming to ask for direction. If Levin had felt good back in the cattle pens and farmyard, he felt even better out in the open. Swaying with the easy rhythm of his cob's gait, breathing in the warm yet fresh scent of the snow and the air, riding through his forest over the crumbling, ragged patches of snow still clinging on here and there, marked with half-melted tracks, he felt a surge of joy over every single tree, over the moss coming back to life on the bark, the buds swelling on every shoot. When he came out of the forest, the vast plain opened up before him, his grasslands stretching out in an unbroken green carpet, with no bare patches or swampy spots, only scattered melting snow left in the hollows. He wasn't even bothered by the sight of the peasants' horses and colts trampling his young grass (he told a peasant he passed to drive them off), or by the dull, sarcastic answer of Ipat, a peasant he ran into on the road, when he asked, "Well, Ipat, will we be sowing soon?" "We need to finish the ploughing first, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," Ipat answered. The farther he rode, the happier he felt, and plans for the land kept forming in his mind, each one better than the last — planting hedges along the southern borders of all his fields so the snow wouldn't drift and settle under them; dividing the land into six fields for crops and three for pasture and hay; building a cattle yard at the far end of the estate; digging a pond; setting up movable pens to help fertilize the land with the cattle. And then eight hundred acres of wheat, three hundred of potatoes, and four hundred of clover — with not a single acre worn out.

Absorbed in these fantasies, carefully steering his horse along the hedges to avoid trampling his young crops, he rode up to the laborers who'd been sent to sow the clover. A cart loaded with seed stood not at the edge of the field but right in the middle of the crop, and the winter wheat had been torn up by the wheels and trampled by the horse. Both laborers were sitting in the hedge, probably sharing a pipe. The soil mixed in with the seed in the cart hadn't been broken down into fine powder — it was still crusted together and clumped. Seeing the master, the laborer Vassily headed toward the cart, while Mishka went on sowing. This wasn't as it should have been, but Levin rarely lost his temper with the laborers. When Vassily came up, Levin told him to lead the horse over to the hedge.
"It's fine, sir, it'll come up anyway," Vassily said.
"Don't argue," Levin said. "Just do as you're told."

"Yes, sir," Vassily answered, taking hold of the horse's head. "What a sowing, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he added, hesitating. "First-rate. Only it's hard going — you drag a ton of earth on your boots."
"Why isn't your soil sifted?" Levin asked.
"Well, we crumble it up by hand," Vassily answered, scooping up some seed and rolling the dirt between his palms.
It wasn't really Vassily's fault that the cart had been loaded with unsifted soil, but it was irritating all the same.

Levin had tried, more than once before, a method he knew for tamping down his anger and turning things back around when they seemed to be going wrong, and he tried it now. He watched Mishka walk along, huge clods of earth swinging off each foot, and, climbing down from his horse, he took the seed-basket from Vassily and started sowing himself.
"Where did you leave off?"

Vassily pointed out the spot with his foot, and Levin set off as best he could, scattering seed over the land. Walking through it was like slogging through a bog, and by the time he finished the row he was sweating heavily, so he stopped and handed the basket back to Vassily.
"Well, master, when summer comes, don't go scolding me for these rows," said Vassily.
"Eh?" Levin said cheerfully, already feeling the effect of his method working on him.

"You'll see once summer's here. It'll look different. Look over there where I sowed last spring. The work I put into it! I do my best, Konstantin Dmitrievitch, same as I would for my own father. I don't like sloppy work, and I won't let anyone else do it either. What's good for the master is good for us too. Just look out there," Vassily said, pointing, "it does your heart good."
"It's a lovely spring, Vassily."

"It's the kind of spring the old men don't even remember the like of. I was up at home — an old fellow there's sown wheat too, about an acre of it. He said you wouldn't be able to tell it apart from rye."
"Have you been sowing wheat long?"
"Well, sir, you're the one who taught us, the year before last. You gave me two measures. We sold off about eight bushels and sowed the rest on a rood."
"Well, make sure you break up the clods," Levin said, heading back to his horse, "and keep an eye on Mishka. And if the crop's good, you'll get half a rouble for every acre."
"Much obliged. We're quite content as it is, sir."
Levin mounted his horse and rode toward the field where last year's clover had grown, and the one already ploughed and ready for spring planting.

The clover coming up through the stubble looked magnificent. It had survived everything, standing up bright green through the broken stalks of last year's wheat. The horse sank in up to the fetlocks, pulling each hoof free with a sucking sound out of the half-thawed ground. Crossing the ploughed field on horseback was completely impossible; the horse could only find footing on the icy patches, sinking deep into the thawing furrows with every step. The ploughland was in excellent shape; in a couple of days it would be ready for harrowing and sowing. Everything was first-rate, everything was cheering him on. Levin rode back across the streams, hoping the water had gone down by now. He did manage to cross, and startled two ducks in the process. "There must be snipe too," he thought, and just as he turned toward home he ran into the forest keeper, who confirmed his hunch about the snipe.
Levin rode home at a trot, wanting to have time for dinner and to get his gun ready for the evening.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Riding back to the house in the best of moods, Levin heard a bell ring at the side of the main entrance.

"That'll be someone from the train station," he thought. "Right about the time for the Moscow train to get in... Who could it be? What if it's my brother Nikolay? He did say: 'Maybe I'll go take the waters, or maybe I'll come stay with you.'" For a moment he felt uneasy and annoyed that his brother's arrival might disturb his happy spring mood. But he felt ashamed of the thought, and immediately, so to speak, opened his arms wide, and with a softened feeling of joy and anticipation, hoped with all his heart that it really was his brother. He spurred his horse on, and riding out from behind the acacia trees, he saw a hired three-horse sledge from the station, and a man in a fur coat. It wasn't his brother. "Oh, if only it were someone pleasant I could talk to a little!" he thought.
"Ah!" Levin cried joyfully, throwing up both hands. "What a wonderful guest! I'm so glad to see you!" he shouted, recognizing Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"I'll find out for certain whether she's married, or when she's going to be," he thought. And on that gorgeous spring day, he felt that even the thought of her didn't hurt at all.

"Well, you didn't expect me, did you?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, climbing out of the sledge, mud splattered across the bridge of his nose, his cheek, and his eyebrows, but glowing with health and good spirits. "First of all, I came to see you," he said, hugging and kissing him, "second, to get some woodcock shooting in, and third, to sell the forest at Ergushovo."
"Wonderful! What a spring we're having! How did you even manage in a sledge?"
"In a cart it would've been even worse, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the driver, who knew him, answered.
"Well, I'm very, very glad to see you," Levin said, with a genuinely delighted, childlike smile.

Levin brought his friend to the guest room, where Stepan Arkadyevitch's things had also been carried — a bag, a gun case, a cigar pouch. Leaving him there to wash up and change, Levin went off to the estate office to talk about the ploughing and the clover. Agafea Mihalovna, always anxious about the household's reputation, met him in the hall with questions about dinner.
"Do whatever you like, just make it quick," he said, and went to find the bailiff.
When he came back, Stepan Arkadyevitch, washed and combed, emerged from his room with a beaming smile, and the two of them went upstairs together.

"Well, I'm glad I finally got away to visit you! Now I'll get to see what mysterious business keeps you so occupied out here. No, really, I envy you. What a house — everything about it is so nice! So bright, so cheerful!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, forgetting that it wasn't always spring and fine weather like today. "And your housekeeper is simply delightful! A pretty maid in an apron might be a bit more fun, maybe, but for your monk-like way of living, she suits perfectly."
Stepan Arkadyevitch shared plenty of interesting news; Levin was especially interested to hear that his brother, Sergey Ivanovitch, was planning to visit him that summer.

Stepan Arkadyevitch didn't say a single word about Kitty or the Shtcherbatskys — only passed along greetings from his wife. Levin was grateful for his tact, and glad to have him as a guest. As always happened during his time alone, a mass of ideas and feelings had been piling up inside him that he'd had no one to share with. And now he poured it all out to Stepan Arkadyevitch — his poetic delight in the spring, his setbacks and plans for the land, his thoughts and criticisms of the books he'd been reading, and the idea for his own book, which was really — though he hadn't quite realized it himself — a critique of every old book ever written on agriculture. Stepan Arkadyevitch, always charming, picking up on everything with the slightest hint, was especially charming on this visit, and Levin noticed in him a kind of special warmth, a new note of respect that he found flattering.

Agafea Mihalovna and the cook worked hard to make dinner especially good, but their efforts only led to the two starving friends tearing through the starter course, eating heaps of bread and butter, salted goose, and pickled mushrooms — enough that Levin ended up ordering the soup served without the little pies the cook had particularly wanted to impress their guest with. But even though Stepan Arkadyevitch was used to very different meals, he found everything wonderful — the herb brandy, the bread, the butter, and above all the salted goose and mushrooms, the nettle soup, the chicken in white sauce, and the white Crimean wine. Every bit of it was superb and delicious.

"Splendid, splendid!" he said, lighting a fat cigar after the roast. "Coming out here feels like landing on a calm shore after the noise and shaking of a steamship. So you're saying the laborer himself is something to study, something that should shape the choice of methods in farming? Of course, I'm an ignorant outsider, but I'd guess theory and its application will end up shaping the laborer too."

"Yes, but wait a minute. I'm not talking about political economy — I'm talking about agricultural science. It should work like the natural sciences: observing the given facts, including the laborer, in his economic and ethnographic context..."
Just then Agafea Mihalovna came in with the jam.
"Oh, Agafea Mihalovna," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, kissing his plump fingertips, "what a goose, what brandy!... So, what do you think — time to head out, Kostya?" he added.
Levin looked out the window at the sun sinking behind the bare treetops of the forest.
"Yes, it's time," he said. "Kouzma, get the trap ready," and he ran downstairs.

On his way down, Stepan Arkadyevitch carefully took the canvas cover off his polished gun case with his own hands and, opening it, began preparing his expensive, latest-model gun. Kouzma, already smelling a good tip, never left Stepan Arkadyevitch's side, helping him on with both his stockings and boots — a job Stepan Arkadyevitch happily let him do.
"Kostya, tell them that if the merchant Ryabinin shows up... I told him to come today... he's to be brought in and told to wait for me..."
"Wait — you're selling the forest to Ryabinin?"
"Yes. Do you know him?"
"Of course I do. I've had to deal with him — 'positively and conclusively.'"
Stepan Arkadyevitch laughed. "Positively and conclusively" were the merchant's favorite words.
"Yes, it's incredibly funny how he talks. She knows exactly where her master's headed!" he added, patting Laska, who hovered around Levin, whining and licking his hands, his boots, and his gun.
The trap was already waiting at the steps when they came out.
"I had them bring the trap round — or would you rather walk?"

"No, let's drive," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, climbing into the trap. He sat down, tucked the tiger-skin rug around himself, and lit a cigar. "How do you not smoke? A cigar is a strange thing — not exactly pleasure itself, but the crowning proof of it. Now this is living! How wonderful! This is how I'd love to live!"
"Well, who's stopping you?" said Levin, smiling.
"No, you're the lucky one! You've got everything you want. You like horses — you have them; dogs — you have them; hunting — you have it; farming — you have it."
"Maybe it's because I enjoy what I have instead of pining for what I don't," Levin said, thinking of Kitty.
Stepan Arkadyevitch understood, glanced at him, but said nothing.

Levin was grateful to Oblonsky for noticing, with his usual tact, that Levin dreaded any talk of the Shtcherbatskys, and for saying nothing about them. But now Levin was desperate to find out what was troubling him so much, and yet he couldn't work up the nerve to ask.
"Come on, tell me how things are going with you," Levin said, realizing it wasn't fair of him to think only about himself.
Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes lit up cheerfully.

"You won't admit, I know, that a man can enjoy fresh rolls once he's already had his ration of bread — to you that's a sin. But I don't count a life without love as living at all," he said, twisting Levin's question to suit himself. "What can I do? That's just how I'm made. And really, it does so little harm to anyone, and it gives me so much pleasure..."
"What — is there something new going on?" Levin asked.

"Yes, my friend, there is! You know the type — women like the ones in Ossian's poems, the kind you see in dreams... Well, sometimes you actually run into women like that in real life... and they're terrifying. A woman, you understand, is the kind of subject that stays perfectly fresh no matter how much you study her."
"Well then, maybe it's better not to study her at all."
"No. Some mathematician once said that the pleasure is in searching for the truth, not in finding it."
Levin listened without a word, and no matter how hard he tried, he couldn't get inside his friend's feelings at all, couldn't understand the appeal of studying women like that.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The spot chosen for the stand-shooting wasn't far above a stream, in a small aspen copse. Once they reached it, Levin got out of the trap and led Oblonsky to a corner of a mossy, swampy clearing already completely clear of snow. He himself went back to a double birch on the other side, leaned his gun against the fork of a dead lower branch, took off his heavy overcoat, refastened his belt, and moved his arms around to check they were free.

Old gray Laska, who'd followed them, sat down cautiously across from him and pricked up her ears. The sun was setting behind a thick forest, and in the glow of the sunset, the birches scattered through the aspen copse stood out sharply, their hanging twigs and swollen buds nearly ready to burst.

From the thickest parts of the copse, where snow still lingered, came the faint sound of thin, winding streams of meltwater trickling away. Small birds twittered, occasionally flitting from tree to tree.
In the moments of total stillness, the rustle of last year's leaves could be heard, stirred by the thawing earth and the grass pushing up beneath them.

"Just imagine — you can actually hear and see the grass growing!" Levin said to himself, noticing a wet, slate-gray aspen leaf shifting beside a blade of young grass. He stood there, listening, his eyes moving from the wet, mossy ground to Laska, alert and listening, to the sea of bare treetops stretching out on the slope below, to the darkening sky streaked with white cloud.

A hawk flew high over a distant stretch of forest, gliding slowly; another followed the exact same path in the exact same direction and vanished. The birds twittered louder and more urgently in the thicket. An owl hooted somewhere nearby, and Laska, startled, took a few careful steps forward, tilted her head to one side, and listened intently. Beyond the stream, a cuckoo called. It gave its usual call twice, then a hoarse, hurried note, and broke off.
"Would you believe it — the cuckoo's already back!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, stepping out from behind a bush.
"Yes, I hear it," Levin answered, reluctant to break the silence with his voice, which sounded unpleasant even to him. "Here it comes!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch's shape disappeared behind the bush again, and all Levin could see was the bright flare of a match, then the red glow and blue smoke of a cigarette.
"Click! Click!" came the sound of Stepan Arkadyevitch cocking his gun.
"What's that cry?" Oblonsky asked, pointing out a long, drawn-out sound, like a colt whinnying playfully in a high voice.
"You don't know that one? That's the hare. But enough talking — listen, it's coming!" Levin almost shouted, cocking his gun.

They heard a sharp whistle in the distance, and — right on the timing every hunter knows by heart — two seconds later came another, then a third, and after the third whistle, the hoarse, throaty cry could be heard.

Levin looked around, right and left, and there, facing him against the darkening blue sky above the tangled mass of young aspen shoots, he spotted the bird in flight. It was heading straight for him; the throaty cry, like the steady tearing of some heavy fabric, sounded right by his ear; he could make out the long beak and neck, and at the exact moment Levin took aim, behind the bush where Oblonsky stood, a flash of red fire went off: the bird dropped like an arrow, then shot back upward. Another red flash came, and the sound of a hit, and the bird, flapping its wings as if trying to hold itself in the air, faltered, hung still for an instant, and dropped with a heavy splash onto the muddy ground.
"Did I miss it?" Stepan Arkadyevitch called out, unable to see through the smoke.

"Here it is!" Levin said, pointing at Laska, who came trotting back slowly, one ear raised, wagging the tip of her shaggy tail, as if trying to stretch out the pleasure, looking almost like she was smiling as she brought the dead bird to her master. "Well, glad you got him," said Levin, though he felt a twinge of envy that he hadn't managed to bag the snipe himself.
"Bad shot from the right barrel," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered, reloading his gun. "Shh — there's another one!"

The sharp whistles came again, one after another. Two snipe, chasing and playing with each other, whistling but not crying out, flew straight at the hunters' heads. Four shots rang out, and the snipe tumbled through the air like swallows before vanishing from sight.

The stand-shooting was excellent. Stepan Arkadyevitch brought down two more birds, and Levin two more, one of which they never found. It started to get dark. Venus, bright and silvery, shone low in the west behind the birch trees with her soft light, and high in the east the red glow of Arcturus twinkled. Overhead, Levin picked out the stars of the Great Bear, then lost them again. The snipe had stopped flying, but Levin decided to wait a little longer, until Venus — which he could see just below a birch branch — rose above it, and until the stars of the Great Bear were perfectly clear. Venus rose above the branch, and the body of the Great Bear, with its long handle, stood out plainly against the dark blue sky, yet still he waited.
"Isn't it time to head home?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
The copse had gone completely quiet now, without a single bird stirring.
"Let's stay a little longer," Levin answered.
"As you like."
They were now standing about fifteen paces apart.
"Stiva!" Levin said suddenly. "Why haven't you told me whether your sister-in-law's married yet, or when she's getting married?"
Levin felt so calm and steady that he imagined no answer could shake him. But he'd never imagined what Stepan Arkadyevitch was about to say.
"She's never thought about getting married, and she's not thinking about it now — she's quite ill, and the doctors have sent her abroad. They're genuinely afraid she may not survive."
"What!" Levin cried. "Seriously ill? What's wrong with her? How did this...?"
While they talked, Laska, ears pricked, was staring up at the sky, then looking at them reproachfully.
"They pick a fine time to chat," she seemed to be thinking. "It's coming — here it is, yes, here it is. They're going to miss it," Laska thought.

But at that exact moment, both of them suddenly heard a sharp whistle that seemed to strike their ears at once, and both grabbed for their guns in the same instant — two flashes lit up, two shots rang out together. The snipe, flying high overhead, instantly folded its wings and dropped into a thicket, bending the delicate young shoots down with it.
"Excellent! Both together!" Levin shouted, and ran with Laska into the thicket to find the bird.
"Oh, right — what was that unpleasant thing?" he thought. "Right, Kitty's sick... Well, nothing to be done about it; I'm truly sorry," he thought.
"She's found it! Isn't she clever?" he said, taking the warm bird from Laska's mouth and tucking it into the nearly full game bag. "Got it, Stiva!" he shouted.
